marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q008.takeaway: Lateral pontine syndrome localizes to lateral pons, usually in AICA territory, and produces crossed sensory findings.
marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q008.displayText: This is lateral pontine syndrome, caused by anterior inferior cerebellar artery territory infarction. Ipsilateral findings may include facial paralysis (CN VII), loss of pain and temperature on the face (CN V), vestibular symptoms such as nystagmus/vertigo/nausea/vomiting/oscillopsia, hearing loss or tinnitus from auditory nerve/cochlear nucleus involvement, and limb or gait ataxia from middle cerebellar peduncle involvement. Contralateral body pain-temperature loss follows spinothalamic involvement. Medial pontine syndrome is associated with paramedian basilar branches and may affect CN VI, vestibular nuclei, middle cerebellar peduncle, corticobulbar and corticospinal tracts.

rationales.a: Medial medulla affects structures such as pyramid and medial lemniscus; ipsilateral facial sensory findings point laterally in pons.
rationales.c: Medial pontine syndrome is associated with paramedian basilar branches and does not explain the crossed lateral-pontine pattern.
rationales.d: Lateral medulla causes Wallenberg syndrome, typically with nucleus ambiguus, spinal trigeminal, spinothalamic, vestibular and inferior cerebellar peduncle findings; facial palsy suggests lateral pons.

marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q009.takeaway: Internal arcuate fibers from nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus cross and form the medial lemniscus.
marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q009.displayText:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of medial lemniscus tract lesion following a high voltage
electrical injury. The medial lemniscus is formed by the internal arcuate fibres. It is also called
Reil's ribbon.
The internal arcuate fibres are axons of the second-order neurons from nucleus gracilis and
nucleus cuneatus. In the upper medulla, they decussate and form the medial lemniscus which
synapses in the thalamus. io"

emphasis: medial lemniscus is formed by the internal arcuate fibres

rationales.a: Anterior external arcuate fibers arise from arcuate nuclei and do not form the medial lemniscus.
rationales.c: Posterior external arcuate fibers are not the decussating second-order dorsal-column axons asked about.
rationales.d: The medial lemniscus forms from internal arcuate fibres, not from external arcuate fibers.

marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q010.takeaway: The olive is a medullary landmark posterolateral to the pyramid.
marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q010.displayText:
The marked structure i.e. olive is seen in the medulla. The external features of medulla oblongata
are:
Anteriorly, the anterior median fissure is continuous with the anterior median fissure of the spinal
cord. On either side of the fissure are pyramids containing the corticospinal tracts. Posterolateral
to the pyramids are olives. Olives are elevations produced by the underlying inferior olivary
nuclei. Posterior to the olives, the inferior cerebellar peduncles connect the medulla with the
cerebellum.
Posteriorly, the superior half forms the floor of the fourth ventricle. Inferiorly, there is a posterior
median sulcus. On either side of this sulcus, the nucleus gracilis is situated. The nucleus cuneatus
lies lateral to nucleus gracilis.
The anterolateral sulcus lies in the groove between the pyramid and the olive and the XII cranial
nerve emerges from there. The posterolateral sulcus lies in the groove between the olives and the

inferior cerebellar peduncles. The IX, X, and XI cranial nerves emerge from here.

marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q011.takeaway: A medullary pyramid lesion above decussation causes contralateral hemiplegia.
marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q011.displayText: The marked medullary pyramid contains the pyramidal (corticospinal) tracts. Before the pyramidal decussation, a lesion causes contralateral hemiplegia.
emphasis: marked medullary pyramid contains the pyramidal (corticospinal) tracts

rationales.b: Ataxia follows cerebellar pathway damage; pyramid contains corticospinal fibers.
rationales.c: Tinnitus may result from auditory pathway involvement, not the medullary pyramid.
rationales.d: Ipsilateral facial palsy points to facial nerve/nucleus involvement in pons, not pyramidal tract damage.

marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q012.takeaway: The dorsal motor vagal nucleus is beneath the fourth-ventricle floor at olivary level.
marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q012.displayText: At the level of the olives, the dorsal motor nucleus of vagus lies beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle. Trapezoid body and superior vestibular nucleus are structures of lower pons, not this medullary section.

rationales.b: Trapezoid body is in pons and participates in auditory pathways.
rationales.c: Superior vestibular nucleus is located in pons; source explicitly contrasts it with the olivary medulla.
rationales.d: Nucleus gracilis is in posterior medulla but not the dorsal nucleus at the ventricular floor asked here.

marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q013.takeaway: Wallenberg syndrome is lateral medullary infarction with nucleus ambiguus and cerebellar pathway findings.
marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q013.displayText: Dysphagia, dysarthria and ataxia with a dorsolateral medullary infarct indicate lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome. Nucleus ambiguus involvement explains dysphagia/dysarthria, and inferior cerebellar peduncle involvement accounts for ataxia. Medial medullary syndrome is Dejerine anterior bulbar syndrome; medullary tegmental paralysis is Babinski–Nageotte syndrome; Weber syndrome is a midbrain syndrome.
emphasis: Medial medullary syndrome is Dejerine anterior bulbar syndrome

rationales.a: Dejerine anterior bulbar syndrome is medial medullary syndrome, not a dorsolateral infarct.
rationales.c: Babinski–Nageotte is medullary tegmental paralysis, not the named lateral medullary syndrome.
rationales.d: Weber syndrome is a midbrain stroke syndrome, not a dorsolateral medullary lesion.

marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q014.takeaway: PICA occlusion can cause Wallenberg syndrome with crossed face-body sensory loss and bulbar symptoms.
marrow__ANAT_CH24_Q014.displayText: Crossed face-body pain-temperature loss with dysphagia and dysarthria indicates lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, classically due to posterior inferior cerebellar artery thrombosis. The lateral medulla is supplied by PICA, a branch of vertebral artery. Findings map to lateral spinothalamic tract (contralateral body loss), spinal trigeminal nucleus (ipsilateral facial loss), vestibular nuclei (vertigo/nausea/vomiting/nystagmus), nucleus ambiguus (dysphagia/dysarthria/hoarseness), and sympathetic fibers (ipsilateral Horner syndrome).

rationales.a: Subclavian artery is not the direct arterial supply to the lateral medulla; vertebral artery gives rise to PICA.
rationales.b: AICA supplies lateral pons and produces lateral pontine syndrome; the bulbar and crossed sensory findings localize to lateral medulla.
rationales.d: Posterior cerebral artery supplies posterior cerebral structures, not the lateral medulla described.
